article_html:
President Donald Trump’s second term has been a wild ride, but his last two years in power could be wilder still if Republicans lose control of Congress in Tuesday’s US midterm elections.

From renewed military action against Iran to election challenges and fightbacks against Democratic investigations, Trump’s post-midterms playbook could involve disruption on all fronts.

Analysts warn that Trump as a “lame duck” president could be the most vengeful Trump of all.

“I’m skeptical that President Trump will go quiet into that good night,” Peter Loge, director of George Washington University’s School of Media and Public Affairs, told AFP.

“There is nothing in history that says he will say ‘I’ve been beaten, my time is over’. Every time Trump has been backed into a corner, he has shouted more and come out fighting.”

Vetoes and vengeance

Trump has always viewed himself as a fighter. He has been clear he will take the same approach if Democrats win one or both chambers of Congress.

“If we didn’t win, I veto everything” in any Democratic legislative agenda, Trump told the New York Post.

The White House says it is also ready to fight back against whatever investigations — or impeachment proceedings — Democrats throw at them.

“They’ll probably go after me, and I’ll go after them,” Trump said in a Time magazine interview. Trump could even direct the Justice Department to investigate Democrats who are probing him.

Trump, who baselessly disputed his 2020 presidential election loss, could also interfere in the midterms by challenging counts or delaying the certification of disputed races.

Iran

Foreign policy is the one area in which lame-duck US presidents still have wide-ranging powers.

Trump may renew large-scale military operations against Iran, although he appeared to indicate on the eve of the midterms that fresh talks could produce a deal.

“I don’t think he wants his legacy to be a warmonger. He wants his legacy to have left America stronger,” Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution told AFP.

Speculation has swirled that Trump could fire Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth as the Iran war drags on — a familiar move for a president who never likes to take the blame.

Ukraine, detente and trade

Trump loves to think of himself as a master of peace deals and is likely to continue to push Ukraine to agree to a settlement with Russia. Fresh trilateral talks are set for next week.

At the same time, Trump will continue to seek detente with the leaders he views as his great power equals — Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The three will potentially meet at a summit in China later this month.

The US is also likely to continue its retrenchment from some of its NATO and other Western allies — and may even accelerate it, said Hass of the Brookings Institution.

On trade, however, Trump would likely remain “unrelentingly active”, as shown by his recent hostility towards Canada, Hass said.

Staying relevant for 2028?

Trump loves being the centre of attention and is unlikely to relish the spotlight turning towards potential successors in the 2028 US presidential election.

Trump — who hosted the reality television show The Apprentice — has been notably coy about backing either Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio for the top job.

But Trump has largely stopped dropping hints at running for a constitutionally-barred third term.

Allan Lichtman, a professor at American University and author of Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation, said Trump would certainly “keep the focus on himself by being the kingmaker.”

Monuments to himself

Like other people getting ready for retirement, Trump may choose to focus on home improvement.

In his closing midterms speech, Trump barely mentioned policy and instead talked about his renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other plans to beautify Washington.

Trump has openly expressed a desire to stamp his own physical mark on Washington because he fears that others will not do it for him.

“We have a lot of great things planned for Washington,” he said at the Reflecting Pool on Monday.

headline: Sarsabz farmers claim all three provincial titles in Punjab's Wheat Yield Competition 2025-26
description: Sarsabz farmers secured first position in 39 out of 40 districts and claimed all three provincial positions.
author: ADVERTORIAL
article_text:
Fatima Fertilizer celebrated farmers’ outstanding achievements at the Sarsabz Ki Jeet Wheat Yield Competition Prize Distribution Ceremony. Farmers using Sarsabz Nitrophos and Calcium Ammonium Nitrate (CAN) secured the top three positions at the provincial level and 119 out of 120 district-level positions in the Punjab Wheat Yield Competition 2025–26, announced by the Government of Punjab.

National Food Security & Research Federal Minister Rana Tanveer Hussain, addressed the ceremony virtually. The event was also attended by Additional Chief Secretary (ACS), Punjab Iftikhar Ali Sahoo; Punjab Secretary Agriculture Shakeel Ahmad Mian and Pakistan Kissan Ittehad President Khalid Khokhar among other dignitaries.

Sarsabz farmers secured first position in 39 out of 40 districts and claimed all three provincial positions. Sajjad Hussain from Muzaffargarh secured first provincial position with a yield of 69 maunds and 39.4 kilograms per acre, followed by Shafiq Ahmed from Attock with 69 maunds and 39.1 kilograms per acre. Muhammad Asghar from Rahim Yar Khan secured third position with 69 maunds and 24.1 kilograms per acre.

As part of the prize distribution, three tractors were awarded to the provincial winners. At the district level, Honda CD 70 motorcycles and LED TVs were presented to all district level positions.

National Food Security & Research Federal Minister Rana Tanveer Hussain addressed the ceremony virtually and said, “I congratulate Fatima Fertilizer and all the farmers using Sarsabz fertilisers on securing all three provincial titles and 119 out of 120 district-level positions in the Punjab Wheat Yield Competition. This remarkable achievement is a source of pride for Pakistan. Increasing wheat production and improving crop yields are essential for strengthening Pakistan’s food security. The government is committed to ensuring the procurement of every grain of wheat in coordination with provincial governments. We are also introducing initiatives to improve farmers’ access to quality seeds, modern technology and agricultural financing. I appreciate Fatima Fertilizer’s efforts in promoting balanced fertiliser use and providing farmers with modern agricultural knowledge and advisory services. The government, private sector, research institutions and farmers must work together to transform agricultural productivity and achieve national food security.”

Additional Chief Secretary (ACS) Punjab Iftikhar Ali Sahoo said that farmers are the backbone of Pakistan’s economy and food security, adding that the government is committed to supporting them through farmer-friendly policies and timely agricultural initiatives. He appreciated Fatima Fertilizer for recognising Punjab’s leading wheat growers and encouraging excellence in agriculture. He said the announced wheat support price of Rs 4,500 per maund, alongside Rs 150 billion in interest-free loans extended to one million farmers through the Kissan Card since October 15, would help farmers access quality seeds and fertilisers on time and strengthen wheat production.

Speaking at the event, Fatima Fertilizer Director Marketing and Sales Rabel Sadozai said, “Last year (2024-25), Sarsabz users also claimed all three provincial positions and 97 of 120 district positions. This year’s results reflect an improvement on last year and highlight the potential to improve wheat produce through balanced crop nutrition and agronomic guidance. Through Sarsabz, we encourage informed farming practices that help farmers make every acre count, strengthen their livelihoods and contribute to Pakistan’s food security.”

The results also highlight the potential to achieve nearly two acres’ worth of national wheat yield from a single acre. While successful Sarsabz farmers recorded yields of approximately 69-70 maunds per acre, the indicative national average stood at around 33 maunds per acre, thus doubling their yield. Fatima Fertilizer supports farmers through agricultural advisory services and soil testing facilities, helping them make informed decisions about their land’s nutritional requirements.”

Through its Sarsabz range, including Nitrophos and CAN, Fatima Fertilizer continues to promote balanced crop nutrition and improved farming practices to help farmers increase productivity and contribute to the country’s food security.

Maaz Sadaqat, Hasan Nawaz named in Pakistan Shaheens squad for Rising Stars Asia Cup
description: Pakistan have been placed in Group ‘B’ alongside India A, Nepal and the United Arab Emirates, while Group ‘A’ comprises Afghanistan A, Bangladesh A, Hong Kong China and Sri Lanka A.
author: Dawn Sport
article_text:
Maaz Sadaqat and Hasan Nawaz have been included in the 15-member Pakistan Shaheens squad for the ACC Men’s Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026, with Abdul Samad appointed captain for the 50-over tournament to be held in Qatar from Nov 19 to 29.

The Pakistan Cricket Board announced the squad on Tuesday, with the Shaheens set to defend the title they won in the previous 50-over edition in 2023. Pakistan are also the defending champions of the T20 version of the competition, having beaten Bangladesh A in a final decided by a Super Over.

The eight-team tournament will feature two groups of four sides. Pakistan have been placed in Group ‘B’ alongside India A, Nepal and the United Arab Emirates, while Group ‘A’ comprises Afghanistan A, Bangladesh A, Hong Kong China and Sri Lanka A.

The Shaheens will open their campaign against the UAE on Nov 20, before taking on India A two days later and Nepal on Nov 24. Their first match will be played at the University of Doha Science and Technology ground, with the remaining group fixtures scheduled at the West End Park International Cricket Stadium.

All three group matches are day-night fixtures except the opening game, which will be played during the day. The semi-finals are scheduled for Nov 26 and 27, with the final to be held on Nov 29.

Samad will lead a batting group that includes Maaz, Hasan, Haider Ali, Shahzaib Khan, Farhan Yousuf and Shamyl Hussain. Rohail Nazir has been named as the designated wicket-keeper.

The squad also includes three spin options in left-arm spin all-rounder Danish Aziz, leg-spinner Saad Masood and Sufyan Moqim. The pace attack will be led by Mohammad Hasnain and also features Ahmed Daniyal, Akif Javed and Muhammad Imran Randhawa.

Ahmed Daniyal was part of the Shaheens side that won the previous T20 edition, playing a key role as the team clinched the title against Bangladesh A in a Super Over.

Pakistan won the last 50-over edition in Sri Lanka in 2023, beating India A by 128 runs in the final. They were runners-up in the opening two editions in 2013 and 2017 before winning the competition in 2019.

The Shaheens will be aiming to retain their title against a field that includes several of the region’s emerging sides, with a meeting against India A among the key fixtures in the group stage.

headline: 'Who cares?' Alaska voters shrug off potential Democratic manipulation
description: Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, in a tight race against Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, is accused of recruiting another Dan Sullivan to run in order to create ballot confusion.
author: AFP
article_text:
In the long line of US midterm voters casting ballots early Monday in Anchorage, Alaska’s largest city, everyone was aware of the whiff of scandal surrounding the election.

Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, in a tight race against Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan that could determine who controls Congress in Washington, stands accused of recruiting another Dan Sullivan to run in order to create ballot confusion and siphon off votes from the senator.

Very few people braving near-freezing conditions in Anchorage appeared concerned about the revelations first reported by The New York Times, which landed like a thunderclap in political circles thousands of miles away.

But in the far northwestern state of Alaska, voter Dale Brown summed up the feeling succinctly: “Who cares?” The 25-year-old carpenter considered the decoy ploy “immoral,” but said he knows “it’s not illegal technically” and that Republicans have used the same tactics, recruiting ghost candidates in Florida’s 2020 Senate race.

“American politics has gone to this absolute dog-and-pony show of lies,” independent voter Brown told AFP, adding: “I think that any kind of moral (conscience) is long gone.”

The controversy “won’t change anything” about his choice though — Brown cast his ballot for Democrats, saying he’s fed up with inflation under President Donald Trump.

Trump has cried foul in Alaska, as the crucial race could cost his party its Senate majority. It is a bitter battle in Anchorage, where rival campaign signs are seen on either side of neighbours’ fences.

‘Pretty clear’

Following the Times account that Peltola’s campaign helped orchestrate the scheme — although the candidate denied any knowledge of it — the president has sought to preemptively challenge the election results.

A federal judge rejected that bid on Sunday, but the pressure from the Trump administration has continued.

Federal authorities have since launched a criminal investigation, although they have refused to explain its legal basis.

At a shopping centre overlooking snow-capped mountains, Rae Hart approached the polling station acknowledging that it could be “confusing potentially” to have a ballot featuring two Dan Sullivans.

But few appeared fooled by the deception, the Republican voter said.

“I heard people in line saying, ‘Be sure to vote for the right Dan Sullivan,’” said Hart, a 37-year-old criminal investigator.

Many voters interviewed by AFP in Alaska said they have been inundated for weeks with flyers, ads and other mail regarding the controversial election.

On the ballot, the Sullivans are clearly distinguishable.

The senator’s name is accompanied by the labels “registered Republican” and “incumbent,” while Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr. — the “fake” Sullivan, as Trump calls him — shows no political affiliation.

Poll workers prepared in advance to answer questions clarifying the situation.

But a volunteer at the polling place confided, on condition of anonymity, that “it seems like people are pretty clear”.

‘Distractive tactics’

Airline pilot Luke Clement agreed, saying: “It’s pretty clear on the ballot who is who.”

The 47-year-old, however, did regret that this year’s campaign has slid into ugly “mudslinging” instead of focusing on the issues.

Clement was particularly concerned about persistent inflation, fueled by Trump’s war on Iran.

Alaskans feel it more acutely than other Americans, he said, because the state’s distance means “everything is shipped in, and everything is dependent on fuel costs”.

Others in line could be heard discussing the decline of salmon populations driven by overfishing and climate change, and the extent to which the state’s vast oil riches should be exploited.

Ultimately, the scandal surrounding Peltola is being used as “distractive tactics” to divert voters away from what’s at stake, said surgical technologist Zara Oakley, 41.

Alaska is seen as a conservative stronghold, but dissatisfaction with Trump is so widespread here that the Senate Democratic challenger is neck-and-neck with the incumbent senator in the polls.

Oakley said she is not surprised Trump is seeking to cast doubt on election results, as he has done in several other US states.

“He seeks to destroy democracy,” she said.

“I don’t think it has anything to do with what is principled or what’s right or what’s just. “

article_html:
In the long line of US midterm voters casting ballots early Monday in Anchorage, Alaska’s largest city, everyone was aware of the whiff of scandal surrounding the election.

Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, in a tight race against Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan that could determine who controls Congress in Washington, stands accused of recruiting another Dan Sullivan to run in order to create ballot confusion and siphon off votes from the senator.

Very few people braving near-freezing conditions in Anchorage appeared concerned about the revelations first reported by The New York Times, which landed like a thunderclap in political circles thousands of miles away.

But in the far northwestern state of Alaska, voter Dale Brown summed up the feeling succinctly: “Who cares?” The 25-year-old carpenter considered the decoy ploy “immoral,” but said he knows “it’s not illegal technically” and that Republicans have used the same tactics, recruiting ghost candidates in Florida’s 2020 Senate race.

“American politics has gone to this absolute dog-and-pony show of lies,” independent voter Brown told AFP, adding: “I think that any kind of moral (conscience) is long gone.”

The controversy “won’t change anything” about his choice though — Brown cast his ballot for Democrats, saying he’s fed up with inflation under President Donald Trump.

Trump has cried foul in Alaska, as the crucial race could cost his party its Senate majority. It is a bitter battle in Anchorage, where rival campaign signs are seen on either side of neighbours’ fences.

‘Pretty clear’

Following the Times account that Peltola’s campaign helped orchestrate the scheme — although the candidate denied any knowledge of it — the president has sought to preemptively challenge the election results.

A federal judge rejected that bid on Sunday, but the pressure from the Trump administration has continued.

Federal authorities have since launched a criminal investigation, although they have refused to explain its legal basis.

At a shopping centre overlooking snow-capped mountains, Rae Hart approached the polling station acknowledging that it could be “confusing potentially” to have a ballot featuring two Dan Sullivans.

But few appeared fooled by the deception, the Republican voter said.

“I heard people in line saying, ‘Be sure to vote for the right Dan Sullivan,’” said Hart, a 37-year-old criminal investigator.

Many voters interviewed by AFP in Alaska said they have been inundated for weeks with flyers, ads and other mail regarding the controversial election.

On the ballot, the Sullivans are clearly distinguishable.

The senator’s name is accompanied by the labels “registered Republican” and “incumbent,” while Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr. — the “fake” Sullivan, as Trump calls him — shows no political affiliation.

Poll workers prepared in advance to answer questions clarifying the situation.

But a volunteer at the polling place confided, on condition of anonymity, that “it seems like people are pretty clear”.

‘Distractive tactics’

Airline pilot Luke Clement agreed, saying: “It’s pretty clear on the ballot who is who.”

The 47-year-old, however, did regret that this year’s campaign has slid into ugly “mudslinging” instead of focusing on the issues.

Clement was particularly concerned about persistent inflation, fueled by Trump’s war on Iran.

Alaskans feel it more acutely than other Americans, he said, because the state’s distance means “everything is shipped in, and everything is dependent on fuel costs”.

Others in line could be heard discussing the decline of salmon populations driven by overfishing and climate change, and the extent to which the state’s vast oil riches should be exploited.

Ultimately, the scandal surrounding Peltola is being used as “distractive tactics” to divert voters away from what’s at stake, said surgical technologist Zara Oakley, 41.

Alaska is seen as a conservative stronghold, but dissatisfaction with Trump is so widespread here that the Senate Democratic challenger is neck-and-neck with the incumbent senator in the polls.

Oakley said she is not surprised Trump is seeking to cast doubt on election results, as he has done in several other US states.

“He seeks to destroy democracy,” she said.

“I don’t think it has anything to do with what is principled or what’s right or what’s just. “

headline: Saudi Aramco profits surge as Middle East war rattles energy markets
description: Saudi oil giant Aramco announced a 34.6 per cent surge in third-quarter net profit, as the Middle East war keeps...
article_text:
Saudi oil giant Aramco announced a 34.6 per cent surge in third-quarter net profit, as the Middle East war keeps crude prices soaring while the kingdom’s energy infrastructure comes under regular attack, Reuters reports.

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have targeted Saudi tankers, pipelines, storage facilities and refineries regularly since hostilities resumed in July, intensifying their strikes in recent weeks.

The kingdom has also had to contend with the Houthis and Iran hampering traffic in the straits of Bab al-Mandeb and Hormuz, complicating exports.

Yet Aramco – the cornerstone of Saudi Arabia’s economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies – saw its profits soar during the third quarter thanks in large part to stubbornly high oil prices.

headline: Australia's Glenn Maxwell calls time on international career
description: He has not been picked since the World Cup in Sri Lanka in February, with selectors bypassing him for a series against Bangladesh in June.
author: AFP
article_text:
Explosive batsman Glenn Maxwell announced his international retirement Tuesday after being overlooked for Australia’s upcoming Twenty20 series against England.

The mercurial 38-year-old, who had not played a Test since 2017, called time on his one-day career last year but kept the door open for T20s.

He has not been picked since the World Cup in Sri Lanka in February, with selectors bypassing him for a series against Bangladesh in June.

Maxwell was again overlooked for the squad named Monday to play England in November, with a host of younger players instead preferred.

“A little bit sad and a little bit inevitable too, but I’m announcing my retirement from international cricket,” Maxwell said on the Final Word podcast.

“We probably had numerous discussions before and after the T20 World Cup,” he added of talks with selectors. “And it was pretty open-ended.

“There wasn’t any pressure from (Australia team management), and we decided to sort of leave the door open.

“There was a couple of series that were coming up (in which) they were going to look to the future, and we saw that in Bangladesh with guys getting their opportunity and performing really well.

“There was a small hope or discussion that I might have been able to potentially get a send-off game at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (against England).

“But I can completely understand the direction they’re going with this squad.” Maxwell played 130 T20 internationals, blasting 2,897 runs with a strike rate of 154.42, leaving as Australia’s third-highest run-scorer after David Warner and Aaron Finch.

While he only played seven Tests, he featured in 149 ODIs, crunching 3,990 runs.

Maxwell also called time on his first-class career with Victoria, but will continue with the Melbourne Renegades in the Big Bash League.

“I’m grateful for the time I was able to play for my country,” he said.

“If you had offered me that career when I first walked into the Victoria change rooms in 2009-ish, I would have bitten your hand off.”

headline: Iran's foreign minister says talks with Saudi Arabia are ongoing; Yemen fighting intensifies
description: Talks between Iran and Saudi Arabia are ongoing as Tehran aims to reach new regional security arrangements for...
article_text:
Talks between Iran and Saudi Arabia are ongoing as Tehran aims to reach new regional security arrangements for countries in the region without foreign military involvement, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Aragchi said on X.

Last week, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran, the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations since August. The US-Israeli war on Iran started in late February and since then, fighting has spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

Riyadh said the visit was intended to open negotiating channels to “prevent the return of military escalation,” as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis had intensified in recent weeks.

Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator in talks with the United States, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said that the ball was in Washington’s court to “prevent war,” AFP reports.

“The countries of the region should know that, just as the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, it has also given the American side a powerful and rational response,” he said in a televised speech. “The ball is now in America’s court to prevent war”.

headline: Lufthansa says 2026 fuel costs to be 2bn euros higher amid Iran war
description: German airline giant Lufthansa said it expects its 2026 fuel costs to be two billion euros ($2.24 billion) higher...
article_text:
German airline giant Lufthansa said it expects its 2026 fuel costs to be two billion euros ($2.24 billion) higher than last year as the Iran war keeps global energy prices elevated, Reuters reports.

Releasing third quarter results, the group predicted its fuel bill across the full year will come in at 9.3 billion euros.

That is 600 million higher than it had anticipated just a few months ago, as the US war against Iran drags on.

The group, which also operates carriers including Swiss, Brussels and Eurowings, also slightly downgraded its forecast for core profit to a range of between 1.7 and 2.0 billion euros for 2026.

Previously it predicted a range of between 1.7 and 2.2 billion euros.

headline: Indian national killed after 2 helicopters collide in Nepal's Mount Everest region
description: Helicopter was carrying passengers who had been rescued from the Everest region when it crashed while landing.
author: Reuters
article_text:
An Indian national was killed and a New Zealander injured after two helicopters collided as they prepared to land in Nepal’s Mount Everest region on Tuesday, authorities said.

The New Zealander has been rescued, the chief district officer of Solukhumbu district, Kaman Singh Thapa Magar, told Reuters. The incident took place in the base camp area of Mount Everest, Magar said.

The helicopters were operated by two private firms, Fishtail Air and Dynasty Air. Fishtail Air said in a statement that its helicopter was carrying passengers who had been rescued from the Everest region when it crashed while landing.

The Indian and the New Zealander on board were tourists, a Fishtail official said, while a Dynasty Air official said its helicopter was carrying only cargo.

The accident comes during the peak trekking season in Nepal, when helicopters ferry hikers and climbers in the region.

Last week, six people were killed in a helicopter crash in the Indian Himalayan state of Uttarakhand. The helicopter was flying from Badrinath, a prominent pilgrimage destination for Hindus located in the mountains, to Dehradun city, the Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority (UCADA) said in a statement.

All six people on board the chopper, including five passengers and the pilot, were killed, ANI reported, citing UCADA’s Chief Executive Officer Prateek Jain.

headline: Asian Cup latest event in Saudi Arabia to be postponed over safety
description: The 2027 Asian Cup football tournament in Saudi Arabia will be postponed from January to December due to...
article_text:
The 2027 Asian Cup football tournament in Saudi Arabia will be postponed from January to December due to “exceptional circumstances” in the region, the continent’s governing body said, Reuters reports.

A number of sports events in Saudi Arabia have been cancelled or postponed in recent weeks following Houthi attacks on the country.

The Asian Cup was originally scheduled to take place from January 7 to February 5 next year.

The new dates for the continental showpiece are December 23, 2027, to January 21, 2028.

“The organising committee for AFC Asian Cup approved to reschedule the flagship national team tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region,” the Asian Football Confederation said in a statement.

headline: Is Rahul Gandhi ambitious?
description: Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him?
author: Jawed Naqvi
article_text:
MILLIONS of Indians evidently see Rahul Gandhi as their candidate to steer the country out of its deep mess driven by hate-filled divisive politics and a K-shaped economic trajectory plying unprecedented inequality. That seemed to be the unspoken sentiment, if not consensus, at the massive Sunday rally of opposition parties in Delhi against vote theft.

The issue has brought out angry youth on the streets. Rigging of polls betrays, however, an inability to secure popular support through clean elections, which is a blessing.

India is not alone in subverting democracy. Narendra Modi’s ride-or-die friendship with Benjamin Netanyahu reveals a shared scorn for secular democracy and minority rights. Netanyahu hopes to disenfranchise Palestinian MPs (strategically called Arabs by a clever political fiat) even as they mock him in turn by holding the balance of power, principally against him, after last week’s elections.

Likewise with Modi, whose controversial victories in Bihar and West Bengal recently benefited enormously as his handpicked election commission disenfranchised millions of Muslim voters and other potential opponents of the regime. Netanyahu rewarded Modi’s friendship by giving his government the Pegasus spyware among other contraptions to undermine democracy.

One would readily go along with the view that Gandhi makes for a great candidate to don the mantle of prime minister and also restore its prestige. He has displayed the drive to nurse Indian democracy back to health. But is he as equipped as, say, streetfighters like Priyank Kharge or M.K. Stalin or Akhilesh Yadav to deal frontally with the push which will inevitably arrive in the process of dismantling entrenched fascism?

That Sonia Gandhi and both her children — Rahul as the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha, Priyanka Gandhi as an outspoken and gritty parliamentarian — called out Israel’s genocide in Gaza, while major parties other than the left looked away is cause to celebrate the family — and also something to worry about as it puts them in the crosshairs of many a foreign and domestic interloper. The fact that the RSS chief hosted an Israeli diplomat as chief guest at the Hindutva body’s annual day on Dussehra is troubling.

Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him?

A pivotal question needs to be flagged here about widespread faux expertise over a future prime minister from the opposition. Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him? A fair guess based on history and Nehru-Gandhi genealogy is that Rahul Gandhi harbours no such ambitions. We could perhaps glean the truth of this hunch from Sonia Gandhi’s soon-to-be released memoirs.

The BJP routinely accuses Jawaharlal Nehru and his daughter of political ambition. No Indian prime minister with a clear majority in parliament has offered to resign other than Nehru. In February 1950, Nehru offered to resign as prime minister over the refugee crisis after Partition. Sardar Patel persuaded him to withdraw the offer. Again, in 1958, Nehru announced his desire to step down and take a break from office, citing severe mental fatigue, fading idealism, and deteriorating public standards in Indian politics. A public outcry broke out, and the Congress begged him to stay on.

Did Nehru want his daughter to succeed him? On the contrary, there’s plenty of evidence that he desired young socialist leader Jai Prakash Narayan as his deputy in 1952, which JP refused. There was not even a remote hint that he wanted his daughter in his cabinet or to succeed him.

Nehru was wary of Morarji Desai from the right-wing of the party. He engineered a plan for senior cabinet ministers to resign to work at the grassroots with the party. He inducted Lal Bahadur Shastri as a minister without portfolio in the prime minister’s office, a clear signal who he was tapping as successor.

Shastri’s demise in Tashkent set off another round of worry about Desai manoeuvring. Powerful regional satraps countered the move and promoted Indira Gandhi believing she could be manipulated. Mrs Gandhi favoured supporting Gulzari Lal Nanda.

The ‘Syndicate’ supporting her was essentially conservative, pro-business, and staunchly anti-socialist. Mrs Gandhi turned the tables on them in 1969 by staging a split with the support of the communist bloc. When the left abandoned her after the emergency — one of their defining errors — she was swamped by the conservatives including religious revivalists who were largely seen as devising her fateful Punjab policy that would eventually lay her low.

Rajiv Gandhi was a scrupulously private family man until Sanjay Gandhi’s death in a plane crash required him to stand with his mother. Her assassination set him up as prime minister. There’s no dearth of recorded evidence of Sonia Gandhi opposing his entry into politics. In an emotional showdown, she forbade him from becoming prime minister, presciently fearing he, too, would be killed. Rajiv’s response was: “I am her son … if I don’t do it, who will?” Ambition?

Did Sonia Gandhi try to be prime minister in 1999 when she met the president with a list of 272 supporters? The world knows that she backed Manmohan Singh as prime minister in 2004. But a 2014 book by R.D. Pradhan, a civil servant close to Rajiv and Sonia Gandhi, described how Sonia Gandhi had Manmohan Singh in mind as early as 1999.

On her part, Sonia Gandhi did one better. The issue has brought out angry youth on the streets. Rigging of polls betrays, however, an inability to secure popular support through clean elections, which is a blessing.

India is not alone in subverting democracy. Narendra Modi’s ride-or-die friendship with Benjamin Netanyahu reveals a shared scorn for secular democracy and minority rights. Netanyahu hopes to disenfranchise Palestinian MPs (strategically called Arabs by a clever political fiat) even as they mock him in turn by holding the balance of power, principally against him, after last week’s elections.

Likewise with Modi, whose controversial victories in Bihar and West Bengal recently benefited enormously as his handpicked election commission disenfranchised millions of Muslim voters and other potential opponents of the regime. Netanyahu rewarded Modi’s friendship by giving his government the Pegasus spyware among other contraptions to undermine democracy.

One would readily go along with the view that Gandhi makes for a great candidate to don the mantle of prime minister and also restore its prestige. He has displayed the drive to nurse Indian democracy back to health. But is he as equipped as, say, streetfighters like Priyank Kharge or M.K. Stalin or Akhilesh Yadav to deal frontally with the push which will inevitably arrive in the process of dismantling entrenched fascism?

That Sonia Gandhi and both her children — Rahul as the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha, Priyanka Gandhi as an outspoken and gritty parliamentarian — called out Israel’s genocide in Gaza, while major parties other than the left looked away is cause to celebrate the family — and also something to worry about as it puts them in the crosshairs of many a foreign and domestic interloper. The fact that the RSS chief hosted an Israeli diplomat as chief guest at the Hindutva body’s annual day on Dussehra is troubling.

Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him?

A pivotal question needs to be flagged here about widespread faux expertise over a future prime minister from the opposition. Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him? A fair guess based on history and Nehru-Gandhi genealogy is that Rahul Gandhi harbours no such ambitions. We could perhaps glean the truth of this hunch from Sonia Gandhi’s soon-to-be released memoirs.

The BJP routinely accuses Jawaharlal Nehru and his daughter of political ambition. No Indian prime minister with a clear majority in parliament has offered to resign other than Nehru. In February 1950, Nehru offered to resign as prime minister over the refugee crisis after Partition. Sardar Patel persuaded him to withdraw the offer. Again, in 1958, Nehru announced his desire to step down and take a break from office, citing severe mental fatigue, fading idealism, and deteriorating public standards in Indian politics. A public outcry broke out, and the Congress begged him to stay on.

He inducted Lal Bahadur Shastri as a minister without portfolio in the prime minister’s office, a clear signal who he was tapping as successor.

The ‘Syndicate’ supporting her was essentially conservative, pro-business, and staunchly anti-socialist. Mrs Gandhi turned the tables on them in 1969 by staging a split with the support of the communist bloc. When the left abandoned her after the emergency — one of their defining errors — she was swamped by the conservatives including religious revivalists who were largely seen as devising her fateful Punjab policy that would eventually lay her low.

Rajiv Gandhi was a scrupulously private family man until Sanjay Gandhi’s death in a plane crash required him to stand with his mother. Her assassination set him up as prime minister. There’s no dearth of recorded evidence of Sonia Gandhi opposing his entry into politics. In an emotional showdown, she forbade him from becoming prime minister, presciently fearing he, too, would be killed. Rajiv’s response was: “I am her son … if I don’t do it, who will?” Ambition?

But a 2014 book by R.D. Pradhan, a civil servant close to Rajiv and Sonia Gandhi, described how Sonia Gandhi had Manmohan Singh in mind as early as 1999.

On her part, Sonia Gandhi did one better. She set up a very effective advisory council to informally but crucially advise the Singh government on progressive issues ranging from poverty alleviation, right to information, right to education, halting disinvestment in public sector undertakings — everything that Nehru and Indira Gandhi would approve of.

Rahul Gandhi would in all likelihood follow the precepts. His politically correct upbringing could struggle against the ugliness of right-wing politics that prompted Nehru to offer to resign. There are many more roughly hewn leaders in the progressive pack to confront an ugly pushback that would come from a cornered fascist order.

headline: Asian Cup postponed until December 2027, AFC says
description: A strike on Riyadh’s international airport last month killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, with Yemen’s Houthi movement claiming responsibility for the attack.
author: Reuters
article_text:
The Asian Cup has been postponed from early 2027 to December next year following recent attacks on hosts Saudi Arabia, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said on Tuesday.

A strike on Riyadh’s international airport last month killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement claiming responsibility for the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

The attacks have continued, with the Houthis saying on Monday they had launched drones towards Dammam airport, raisingmore questions over whether the Asian Cup could still go ahead as scheduled from January 7 to February 5.

On Tuesday, the AFC said the 24-team tournament would now take place from December 23 next year to January 21, 2028.

The competition’s organising committee said the tournament had been rescheduled in light of the “exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions”.

“The new dates of the tournament will be presented to FIFA for approval,” it added. “Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders.”

SAUDI ‘FULLY PREPARED’ TO HOST

Yasser Al-Misehal, head of the local organising committee for the Asian Cup, said Saudi Arabia had been fully prepared to host the tournament as scheduled.

“We will continue our work with the same momentum leading up to the tournament’s new dates in December 2027,” Al-Misehal told the Saudi state news agency.

“We are working closely with the AFC and all our partners to ensure a seamless, high-standard organizational experience, and to deliver an exceptional edition worthy of both the kingdoms stature and the AFC Asian Cup.”

The Saudi government has invested heavily in sport through its Public Investment Fund in recent years and the Asian Cup was pitched as an early rehearsal for hosting the World Cup in 2034.

Saudi Arabia have won the Asian Cup three times but have never hosted the continental tournament.

The Asian Cup, traditionally staged in odd-numbered years, had been set to switch to an even-year cycle beginning with the 2032 tournament.

Disruptions in travel and security concerns have affected other sporting events in Saudi Arabia, with golf’s Asian Tour postponing the Saudi International indefinitely, while cycling’s Urban World Championships were also cancelled.

The Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has been moved from October to December and world soccer governing body FIFA postponed the FIFAe Finals 2026 video game competition in Jeddah until an unspecified future date.

Not all sport in the kingdom has been called off, however, with Saul “Canelo” Alvarez beating Christian Mbilli in their world title bout in Riyadh on Saturday

headline: Is Rahul Gandhi ambitious?
description: Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him?
author: Jawed Naqvi
article_text:
MILLIONS of Indians evidently see Rahul Gandhi as their candidate to steer the country out of its deep mess driven by hate-filled divisive politics and a K-shaped economic trajectory plying unprecedented inequality. That seemed to be the unspoken sentiment, if not consensus, at the massive Sunday rally of opposition parties in Delhi against vote theft.

The issue has brought out angry youth on the streets. Rigging of polls betrays, however, an inability to secure popular support through clean elections, which is a blessing.

India is not alone in subverting democracy. Narendra Modi’s ride-or-die friendship with Benjamin Netanyahu reveals a shared scorn for secular democracy and minority rights. Netanyahu hopes to disenfranchise Palestinian MPs (strategically called Arabs by a clever political fiat) even as they mock him in turn by holding the balance of power, principally against him, after last week’s elections.

Likewise with Modi, whose controversial victories in Bihar and West Bengal recently benefited enormously as his handpicked election commission disenfranchised millions of Muslim voters and other potential opponents of the regime. Netanyahu rewarded Modi’s friendship by giving his government the Pegasus spyware among other contraptions to undermine democracy.

One would readily go along with the view that Gandhi makes for a great candidate to don the mantle of prime minister and also restore its prestige. He has displayed the drive to nurse Indian democracy back to health. But is he as equipped as, say, streetfighters like Priyank Kharge or M.K. Stalin or Akhilesh Yadav to deal frontally with the push which will inevitably arrive in the process of dismantling entrenched fascism?

That Sonia Gandhi and both her children — Rahul as the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha, Priyanka Gandhi as an outspoken and gritty parliamentarian — called out Israel’s genocide in Gaza, while major parties other than the left looked away is cause to celebrate the family — and also something to worry about as it puts them in the crosshairs of many a foreign and domestic interloper. The fact that the RSS chief hosted an Israeli diplomat as chief guest at the Hindutva body’s annual day on Dussehra is troubling.

Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him?

A pivotal question needs to be flagged here about widespread faux expertise over a future prime minister from the opposition. Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him? A fair guess based on history and Nehru-Gandhi genealogy is that Rahul Gandhi harbours no such ambitions. We could perhaps glean the truth of this hunch from Sonia Gandhi’s soon-to-be released memoirs.

The BJP routinely accuses Jawaharlal Nehru and his daughter of political ambition. No Indian prime minister with a clear majority in parliament has offered to resign other than Nehru. In February 1950, Nehru offered to resign as prime minister over the refugee crisis after Partition. Sardar Patel persuaded him to withdraw the offer. Again, in 1958, Nehru announced his desire to step down and take a break from office, citing severe mental fatigue, fading idealism, and deteriorating public standards in Indian politics. A public outcry broke out, and the Congress begged him to stay on.

Did Nehru want his daughter to succeed him? On the contrary, there’s plenty of evidence that he desired young socialist leader Jai Prakash Narayan as his deputy in 1952, which JP refused. There was not even a remote hint that he wanted his daughter in his cabinet or to succeed him.

Nehru was wary of Morarji Desai from the right-wing of the party. He engineered a plan for senior cabinet ministers to resign to work at the grassroots with the party. He inducted Lal Bahadur Shastri as a minister without portfolio in the prime minister’s office, a clear signal who he was tapping as successor.

Shastri’s demise in Tashkent set off another round of worry about Desai manoeuvring. Powerful regional satraps countered the move and promoted Indira Gandhi believing she could be manipulated. Mrs Gandhi favoured supporting Gulzari Lal Nanda.

The ‘Syndicate’ supporting her was essentially conservative, pro-business, and staunchly anti-socialist. Mrs Gandhi turned the tables on them in 1969 by staging a split with the support of the communist bloc. When the left abandoned her after the emergency — one of their defining errors — she was swamped by the conservatives including religious revivalists who were largely seen as devising her fateful Punjab policy that would eventually lay her low.

Rajiv Gandhi was a scrupulously private family man until Sanjay Gandhi’s death in a plane crash required him to stand with his mother. Her assassination set him up as prime minister. There’s no dearth of recorded evidence of Sonia Gandhi opposing his entry into politics. In an emotional showdown, she forbade him from becoming prime minister, presciently fearing he, too, would be killed. Rajiv’s response was: “I am her son … if I don’t do it, who will?” Ambition?

Did Sonia Gandhi try to be prime minister in 1999 when she met the president with a list of 272 supporters? The world knows that she backed Manmohan Singh as prime minister in 2004. But a 2014 book by R.D. Pradhan, a civil servant close to Rajiv and Sonia Gandhi, described how Sonia Gandhi had Manmohan Singh in mind as early as 1999.

On her part, Sonia Gandhi did one better. She set up a very effective advisory council to informally but crucially advise the Singh government on progressive issues ranging from poverty alleviation, right to information, right to education, halting disinvestment in public sector undertakings — everything that Nehru and Indira Gandhi would approve of.

Rahul Gandhi would in all likelihood follow the precepts. His politically correct upbringing could struggle against the ugliness of right-wing politics that prompted Nehru to offer to resign. There are many more roughly hewn leaders in the progressive pack to confront an ugly pushback that would come from a cornered fascist order.

The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.

Netanyahu rewarded Modi’s friendship by giving his government the Pegasus spyware among other contraptions to undermine democracy.

He has displayed the drive to nurse Indian democracy back to health. But is he as equipped as, say, streetfighters like Priyank Kharge or M.K. Stalin or Akhilesh Yadav to deal frontally with the push which will inevitably arrive in the process of dismantling entrenched fascism?

That Sonia Gandhi and both her children — Rahul as the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha, Priyanka Gandhi as an outspoken and gritty parliamentarian — called out Israel’s genocide in Gaza, while major parties other than the left looked away is cause to celebrate the family — and also something to worry about as it puts them in the crosshairs of many a foreign and domestic interloper. The fact that the RSS chief hosted an Israeli diplomat as chief guest at the Hindutva body’s annual day on Dussehra is troubling.

Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him?

A pivotal question needs to be flagged here about widespread faux expertise over a future prime minister from the opposition. Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him? A fair guess based on history and Nehru-Gandhi genealogy is that Rahul Gandhi harbours no such ambitions. We could perhaps glean the truth of this hunch from Sonia Gandhi’s soon-to-be released memoirs.

The BJP routinely accuses Jawaharlal Nehru and his daughter of political ambition. No Indian prime minister with a clear majority in parliament has offered to resign other than Nehru. In February 1950, Nehru offered to resign as prime minister over the refugee crisis after Partition. Sardar Patel persuaded him to withdraw the offer. Again, in 1958, Nehru announced his desire to step down and take a break from office, citing severe mental fatigue, fading idealism, and deteriorating public standards in Indian politics. A public outcry broke out, and the Congress begged him to stay on.

Nehru was wary of Morarji Desai from the right-wing of the party. He engineered a plan for senior cabinet ministers to resign to work at the grassroots with the party. He inducted Lal Bahadur Shastri as a minister without portfolio in the prime minister’s office, a clear signal who he was tapping as successor.

Shastri’s demise in Tashkent set off another round of worry about Desai manoeuvring. Powerful regional satraps countered the move and promoted Indira Gandhi believing she could be manipulated. Mrs Gandhi favoured supporting Gulzari Lal Nanda.

The ‘Syndicate’ supporting her was essentially conservative, pro-business, and staunchly anti-socialist. Mrs Gandhi turned the tables on them in 1969 by staging a split with the support of the communist bloc. When the left abandoned her after the emergency — one of their defining errors — she was swamped by the conservatives including religious revivalists who were largely seen as devising her fateful Punjab policy that would eventually lay her low.

Rajiv Gandhi was a scrupulously private family man until Sanjay Gandhi’s death in a plane crash required him to stand with his mother. Her assassination set him up as prime minister. There’s no dearth of recorded evidence of Sonia Gandhi opposing his entry into politics. In an emotional showdown, she forbade him from becoming prime minister, presciently fearing he, too, would be killed. Rajiv’s response was: “I am her son … if I don’t do it, who will?” Ambition?

Did Sonia Gandhi try to be prime minister in 1999 when she met the president with a list of 272 supporters? The world knows that she backed Manmohan Singh as prime minister in 2004. But a 2014 book by R.D. Pradhan, a civil servant close to Rajiv and Sonia Gandhi, described how Sonia Gandhi had Manmohan Singh in mind as early as 1999.

On her part, Sonia Gandhi did one better. She set up a very effective advisory council to informally but crucially advise the Singh government on progressive issues ranging from poverty alleviation, right to information, right to education, halting disinvestment in public sector undertakings — everything that Nehru and Indira Gandhi would approve of.

Rahul Gandhi would in all likelihood follow the precepts. His politically correct upbringing could struggle against the ugliness of right-wing politics that prompted Nehru to offer to resign. There are many more roughly hewn leaders in the progressive pack to confront an ugly pushback that would come from a cornered fascist order.

The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.

headline: Oil rises as peace prospects dim after US hits Iran's Qeshm Island
description: Oil prices rose more than $1, as an Iranian official said a deal to the end the war was far off, while the United...
article_text:
Oil prices rose more than $1, as an Iranian official said a deal to the end the war was far off, while the United States struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, fuelling concerns over the escalation of hostilities and risks to energy supplies, Reuters reports.

US West Texas Intermediate crude was up $1.6, or 1.66 per cent, at $98.06 a barrel while Brent crude futures rose $1.84, or 1.76pc, to $106.61 a barrel by 0744 GMT.

Both benchmarks had dropped more than 7pc on Monday as talks between Iranian and Qatar officials lifted hopes for an end to the US-Israeli war with Iran that were soon dashed.

headline: The American midterm elections as explained by a Pakistani journalist
description: Witnessing a democracy in action, when you’ve never lived in one before
author: Areeba Fatima
article_text:
My first encounter with democracy outside Pakistan took place on a freezing American night whose headlines rocked the world. Thirty-four-year-old Muslim democrat socialist, Zohran Mamdani, had beaten well-funded establishment figure Andrew Cuomo and was delivering his victory speech at the Brooklyn Paramount theatre as the mayor of New York. For someone like me, who had just covered a general election in Pakistan, this was brain-altering.

I had come to the US to pursue a Master’s in data journalism and continue reporting. I had just published a comprehensive account of the widely alleged rigging in Pakistan’s general election 2024. And so I was even more keenly watching the lead-up to the New York mayoral race, how it unfolded, was reported and analysed. Thus far, the president had called the candidate “a Communist Lunatic,” questioned his American citizenship, and called Jews who voted for him “Jew haters.”

Donald Trump, a Queens native, and technically the most powerful person in the country, had been consumed by a bubbling hatred for Mamdani. Despite all that, Mamdani won, and in his first meeting as mayor of Trump’s city, at the Oval Office, Mamdani charmed Trump so thoroughly that when a reporter asked Mamdani whether he still considered the president a fascist, Trump told the young mayor he could just say yes. Speaking to the press on Nov 21, Trump congratulated the mayor-elect and expressed his desire to help the city beat the rising affordability crisis, Mamdani’s biggest campaign promise.

Even the most powerful person in the country was ultimately powerless before the people’s mandate.

Now I have the opportunity to report on another general election, the one the Americans call the midterms.

What are the midterms?

America’s central or federal arm of government that makes laws is called Congress, and like Pakistan’s Parliament, it has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The House is roughly the equivalent of our National Assembly. Its 435 members are elected from districts drawn by population, and each member serves a two-year term, so every seat is contested every two years.

The Senate has 100 members, two from each state regardless of size, serving staggered six-year terms, so about a third of these seats are up at each election. Unlike our Senate, which is chosen by the provincial assemblies, American senators are elected directly by voters.

Presidential elections are held every four years in the US. The congressional elections that fall halfway through a president’s term are called the midterms.

The midterms decide whether the Democrats (blue) or the Republicans (red) will control Congress for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term. This will impact how Trump is able to implement decisions until the next presidential election in 2028.

Midterms are widely read as a referendum on the sitting president, and it appears Trump is not doing very well.

His approval fell to its lowest point of his second term after the US and Israel launched coordinated strikes on Iran on February 28, leading to rising fuel prices and cost of living.

By fall, America’s war with Iran became the most unpopular policy decision made by this Republican administration, with 65 per cent of Americans disapproving of Trump’s handling of the Iran conflict, according to the Pew Research Center.

A blue or Democrat-heavy Congress could open investigations into allegations of corruption against the president, push for the release of the remaining Epstein files, block funding for Trump’s illegal war in Iran, and determine the status of the American people’s access to healthcare among several significant policy decisions.

Who is on the ballot?

All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs, while 35 of 100 seats in the Senate are being contested. As of Tuesday, the Republicans hold 53 of the Senate’s 100 seats, so the Democrats need a net gain of four to reach a majority. A 50-50 split would leave the Republican vice president, JD Vance, with the tie-breaking votes.

In the House, Republicans hold a narrow 218-214 majority, and 218 seats are needed to control the chamber.

Apart from the Congressional election, the gubernatorial race will also play out in 36 states, including California, Florida, Georgia, and Michigan.

In Pakistan, party leadership hands out tickets to candidates they want to field in the constituencies. In America, voters choose each party’s nominee in an earlier election called a primary.

What do the forecasts say?

In functional democracies, statisticians, data journalists, and pollsters put their heads together, survey the population and create a bloated economy of its own.

North America accounts for a whopping 42 per cent of the global polling market, according to a January 2026 report by Research and Markets.

Nate Silver, America’s most popular election bookie and founder of the now defunct FiveThirtyEight, gives Democrats a 95 per cent chance of retaking the House and a 77.7 per cent chance of winning back the Senate. National polls two days out had Democrats at 51.5 per cent and Republicans at 43.1.

A lot of states allow voters to vote before election day or mail their signed ballots, this generally helps elderly voters participate and increase the overall turnout for elections. With more than 53 million Americans voting early by Sunday morning, it appears the forecasters are predicting a blue tsunami.

What makes this year unusual is where the fight is happening. The states Trump won by double digits in 2024 are now being slated for a Democratic flip. Drop Site News reports that rural voters, by staying home or switching sides, could cost Republican Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, Texas, Alaska, and even Florida and Mississippi.

Money in politics

Unlike in Pakistan, where campaign financing is largely opaque, granular data exists in the US to show campaign contributions.

Candidates raise funds directly, although under limits. Super PACs (Political Action Committees), created after a 2010 Supreme Court ruling, can raise and spend unlimited amounts as long as they don’t coordinate with campaigns, and they must report their spending to the Federal Election Commission.

The most important group making political contributions is the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), whose super PAC is called United Democracy Project (UDP).

In 2025-2026, UDP alone made political contributions worth over $108 million, according to their Federal Election Commission filings, and almost all of it was spent on Democratic primaries. This shows both that AIPAC is able to influence the Democrats just as much as Republicans and that they are also expecting a blue wave.

Key Senate races

Michigan has become the most expensive test of pro-Israel political money in the country. In the Democratic primary, UDP spent more than $20 million against Abdul El-Sayed, a physician, former head of Detroit’s health department, and vocal critic of Israel’s war on Gaza, and more than $10 million supporting his rival, Representative Haley Stevens. El-Sayed won by about 14,000 votes.

Stevens, who lost the primary to El-Sayed, spent three months refusing to endorse him. She eventually appeared with Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate fighting El-Sayed, and endorsed Rogers instead, a move Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called a “despicable betrayal.”

Despite incurring serious damage to her own reputation within the party, Stevens’ decision to endorse Mike Rogers against El-Sayed has surprised everyone. It is an exceedingly rare political event historically for sitting Democrats to cross party lines to endorse Republicans after a primary loss.

El-Sayed had appeared on the campaign trail with Barack Obama and Kamala Harris, illustrating the Democratic Party establishment’s support behind his campaign.

Another significant race is taking place in Maine, where Republican Susan Collins is seeking a sixth term against Democratic nominee Troy Jackson.

Troy Jackson is a logger from Allagash and a former president of the Maine Senate. He didn’t even win the primary for his seat, which was handed to him when the original nominee, Graham Platner, was forced to withdraw over allegations of sexual assault, which he denies.

Jackson now has a 6-point lead in the polls.

In South Carolina, Lindsey Graham, the state’s senator for more than two decades, died celebrating Trump’s illegal war on Iran. The baton was naturally passed to his younger sister, Darline Graham.

Alaska has two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the ballot: the Republican incumbent and a retired schoolteacher who, according to a New York Times investigation, was recruited as a spoiler candidate by aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. She has denied knowing anything about the effort. The New York Times noted that ballot stacking is legal and has been used by both parties in Alaska, and its investigation did not establish any criminal wrongdoing.

The House, the redistricting and a rising American left

Unlike the Senate, all 435 House seats are up for election, and Republicans are clinging to a 218-214 majority. But the congressional districts look considerably different in 2026.

But many districts look different this year, because several states redrew their maps mid-decade to favour one party, a practice known as gerrymandering.

Trump forced Texas to add five additional seats for the Republicans, and Florida to add four. He also made Tennessee cut through the last Black-majority district. Californian Democrats have responded by carving out five new districts of their own.

In Pakistan, constituency boundaries are drawn by the Election Commission after each census, and the 2023 delimitation was contested in its own right. In America, state legislatures, which means politicians, draw the lines themselves.

Despite the redraws, the national environment favours Democrats; among those are candidates endorsed by groups such as Justice Democrats (JD) and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). These progressive groups have also backed rising candidates such as Mamdani.

Justice Democrats was responsible for recruiting Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the waitress-turned-politician who might now be eyeing the 2028 presidential race. This cycle, Justice Democrats endorsed 15 candidates; seven won, three of them by unseating sitting members of Congress.

Former Columbia University encampment organiser Darializa Avila Chevalier managed to unseat Adriano Espaillat in New York City. Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old lawyer fired from her firm for her advocacy for Palestine, toppled the 30-year incumbent in Denver.

With Mamdani’s endorsement, union organiser Claire Valdez won the primary in Queens, New York City. Barring an asteroid, these young politicians will make their congressional debut. And when they win, they will be seated, sworn in.

While Trump refused to accept his 2020 defeat, and his supporters stormed the Capitol on January 6, 2021, the courts held them accountable, and power changed hands. It was only when Trump was re-elected in 2024, he pardoned the Jan 6 rioters en masse.

The United States has the most powerful military in human history, and it is nowhere to be found near the electoral process.

No matter who the American people eventually end up coming out for, come Nov 3, some of the most powerful people in the country will lose, and they will stand in front of the media, accept defeat, and live to fight another day in the court of public opinion. Abdul El-Sayed might win or lose, but he will not end up behind bars, soon to be joined by his family members, just because he dared to believe a vote could change a nation’s destiny.

article_html:
My first encounter with democracy outside Pakistan took place on a freezing American night whose headlines rocked the world. Thirty-four-year-old Muslim democrat socialist, Zohran Mamdani, had beaten well-funded establishment figure Andrew Cuomo and was delivering his victory speech at the Brooklyn Paramount theatre as the mayor of New York. For someone like me, who had just covered a general election in Pakistan, this was brain-altering.

I had come to the US to pursue a Master’s in data journalism and continue reporting. I had just published a comprehensive account of the widely alleged rigging in Pakistan’s general election 2024. And so I was even more keenly watching the lead-up to the New York mayoral race, how it unfolded, was reported and analysed. Thus far, the president had called the candidate “a Communist Lunatic,” questioned his American citizenship, and called Jews who voted for him “Jew haters.”

Donald Trump, a Queens native, and technically the most powerful person in the country, had been consumed by a bubbling hatred for Mamdani. Despite all that, Mamdani won, and in his first meeting as mayor of Trump’s city, at the Oval Office, Mamdani charmed Trump so thoroughly that when a reporter asked Mamdani whether he still considered the president a fascist, Trump told the young mayor he could just say yes. Speaking to the press on Nov 21, Trump congratulated the mayor-elect and expressed his desire to help the city beat the rising affordability crisis, Mamdani’s biggest campaign promise.

Even the most powerful person in the country was ultimately powerless before the people’s mandate.

Now I have the opportunity to report on another general election, the one the Americans call the midterms.

What are the midterms?

America’s central or federal arm of government that makes laws is called Congress, and like Pakistan’s Parliament, it has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The House is roughly the equivalent of our National Assembly. Its 435 members are elected from districts drawn by population, and each member serves a two-year term, so every seat is contested every two years.

The Senate has 100 members, two from each state regardless of size, serving staggered six-year terms, so about a third of these seats are up at each election. Unlike our Senate, which is chosen by the provincial assemblies, American senators are elected directly by voters.

Presidential elections are held every four years in the US. The congressional elections that fall halfway through a president’s term are called the midterms.

The midterms decide whether the Democrats (blue) or the Republicans (red) will control Congress for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term. This will impact how Trump is able to implement decisions until the next presidential election in 2028.

Midterms are widely read as a referendum on the sitting president, and it appears Trump is not doing very well.

His approval fell to its lowest point of his second term after the US and Israel launched coordinated strikes on Iran on February 28, leading to rising fuel prices and cost of living.

By fall, America’s war with Iran became the most unpopular policy decision made by this Republican administration, with 65 per cent of Americans disapproving of Trump’s handling of the Iran conflict, according to the Pew Research Center.

A blue or Democrat-heavy Congress could open investigations into allegations of corruption against the president, push for the release of the remaining Epstein files, block funding for Trump’s illegal war in Iran, and determine the status of the American people’s access to healthcare among several significant policy decisions.

Who is on the ballot?

All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs, while 35 of 100 seats in the Senate are being contested. As of Tuesday, the Republicans hold 53 of the Senate’s 100 seats, so the Democrats need a net gain of four to reach a majority. A 50-50 split would leave the Republican vice president, JD Vance, with the tie-breaking votes.

In the House, Republicans hold a narrow 218-214 majority, and 218 seats are needed to control the chamber.

Apart from the Congressional election, the gubernatorial race will also play out in 36 states, including California, Florida, Georgia, and Michigan.

In Pakistan, party leadership hands out tickets to candidates they want to field in the constituencies. In America, voters choose each party’s nominee in an earlier election called a primary.

What do the forecasts say?

In functional democracies, statisticians, data journalists, and pollsters put their heads together, survey the population and create a bloated economy of its own.

North America accounts for a whopping 42 per cent of the global polling market, according to a January 2026 report by Research and Markets.

Nate Silver, America’s most popular election bookie and founder of the now defunct FiveThirtyEight, gives Democrats a 95 per cent chance of retaking the House and a 77.7 per cent chance of winning back the Senate. National polls two days out had Democrats at 51.5 per cent and Republicans at 43.1.

A lot of states allow voters to vote before election day or mail their signed ballots, this generally helps elderly voters participate and increase the overall turnout for elections. With more than 53 million Americans voting early by Sunday morning, it appears the forecasters are predicting a blue tsunami.

What makes this year unusual is where the fight is happening. The states Trump won by double digits in 2024 are now being slated for a Democratic flip. Drop Site News reports that rural voters, by staying home or switching sides, could cost Republican Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, Texas, Alaska, and even Florida and Mississippi.

Money in politics

Unlike in Pakistan, where campaign financing is largely opaque, granular data exists in the US to show campaign contributions.

Candidates raise funds directly, although under limits. Super PACs (Political Action Committees), created after a 2010 Supreme Court ruling, can raise and spend unlimited amounts as long as they don’t coordinate with campaigns, and they must report their spending to the Federal Election Commission.

The most important group making political contributions is the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), whose super PAC is called United Democracy Project (UDP).

In 2025-2026, UDP alone made political contributions worth over $108 million, according to their Federal Election Commission filings, and almost all of it was spent on Democratic primaries. This shows both that AIPAC is able to influence the Democrats just as much as Republicans and that they are also expecting a blue wave.

Key Senate races

Michigan has become the most expensive test of pro-Israel political money in the country. In the Democratic primary, UDP spent more than $20 million against Abdul El-Sayed, a physician, former head of Detroit’s health department, and vocal critic of Israel’s war on Gaza, and more than $10 million supporting his rival, Representative Haley Stevens. El-Sayed won by about 14,000 votes.

Stevens, who lost the primary to El-Sayed, spent three months refusing to endorse him. She eventually appeared with Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate fighting El-Sayed, and endorsed Rogers instead, a move Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called a “despicable betrayal.”

Despite incurring serious damage to her own reputation within the party, Stevens’ decision to endorse Mike Rogers against El-Sayed has surprised everyone. It is an exceedingly rare political event historically for sitting Democrats to cross party lines to endorse Republicans after a primary loss.

El-Sayed had appeared on the campaign trail with Barack Obama and Kamala Harris, illustrating the Democratic Party establishment’s support behind his campaign.

Another significant race is taking place in Maine, where Republican Susan Collins is seeking a sixth term against Democratic nominee Troy Jackson.

Troy Jackson is a logger from Allagash and a former president of the Maine Senate. He didn’t even win the primary for his seat, which was handed to him when the original nominee, Graham Platner, was forced to withdraw over allegations of sexual assault, which he denies.

Jackson now has a 6-point lead in the polls.

In South Carolina, Lindsey Graham, the state’s senator for more than two decades, died celebrating Trump’s illegal war on Iran. The baton was naturally passed to his younger sister, Darline Graham.

Alaska has two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the ballot: the Republican incumbent and a retired schoolteacher who, according to a New York Times investigation, was recruited as a spoiler candidate by aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. She has denied knowing anything about the effort. The New York Times noted that ballot stacking is legal and has been used by both parties in Alaska, and its investigation did not establish any criminal wrongdoing.

The House, the redistricting and a rising American left

Unlike the Senate, all 435 House seats are up for election, and Republicans are clinging to a 218-214 majority. But the congressional districts look considerably different in 2026.

But many districts look different this year, because several states redrew their maps mid-decade to favour one party, a practice known as gerrymandering.

Trump forced Texas to add five additional seats for the Republicans, and Florida to add four. He also made Tennessee cut through the last Black-majority district. Californian Democrats have responded by carving out five new districts of their own.

In Pakistan, constituency boundaries are drawn by the Election Commission after each census, and the 2023 delimitation was contested in its own right. In America, state legislatures, which means politicians, draw the lines themselves.

Despite the redraws, the national environment favours Democrats; among those are candidates endorsed by groups such as Justice Democrats (JD) and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). These progressive groups have also backed rising candidates such as Mamdani.

Justice Democrats was responsible for recruiting Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the waitress-turned-politician who might now be eyeing the 2028 presidential race. This cycle, Justice Democrats endorsed 15 candidates; seven won, three of them by unseating sitting members of Congress.

Former Columbia University encampment organiser Darializa Avila Chevalier managed to unseat Adriano Espaillat in New York City. Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old lawyer fired from her firm for her advocacy for Palestine, toppled the 30-year incumbent in Denver.

With Mamdani’s endorsement, union organiser Claire Valdez won the primary in Queens, New York City. Barring an asteroid, these young politicians will make their congressional debut. And when they win, they will be seated, sworn in.

While Trump refused to accept his 2020 defeat, and his supporters stormed the Capitol on January 6, 2021, the courts held them accountable, and power changed hands. It was only when Trump was re-elected in 2024, he pardoned the Jan 6 rioters en masse.

The United States has the most powerful military in human history, and it is nowhere to be found near the electoral process.

No matter who the American people eventually end up coming out for, come Nov 3, some of the most powerful people in the country will lose, and they will stand in front of the media, accept defeat, and live to fight another day in the court of public opinion. Abdul El-Sayed might win or lose, but he will not end up behind bars, soon to be joined by his family members, just because he dared to believe a vote could change a nation’s destiny.

Midterms are widely read as a referendum on the sitting president, and it appears Trump is not doing very well.

His approval fell to its lowest point of his second term after the US and Israel launched coordinated strikes on Iran on February 28, leading to rising fuel prices and cost of living.

By fall, America’s war with Iran became the most unpopular policy decision made by this Republican administration, with 65 per cent of Americans disapproving of Trump’s handling of the Iran conflict, according to the Pew Research Center.

A blue or Democrat-heavy Congress could open investigations into allegations of corruption against the president, push for the release of the remaining Epstein files, block funding for Trump’s illegal war in Iran, and determine the status of the American people’s access to healthcare among several significant policy decisions.

All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs, while 35 of 100 seats in the Senate are being contested. As of Tuesday, the Republicans hold 53 of the Senate’s 100 seats, so the Democrats need a net gain of four to reach a majority. In the House, Republicans hold a narrow 218-214 majority, and 218 seats are needed to control the chamber.

In functional democracies, statisticians, data journalists, and pollsters put their heads together, survey the population and create a bloated economy of its own.
